claims.text: Integrating in-situ high-temperature neutron imaging with third-generation CALPHAD can accurately and efficiently determine fusion and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a broad range of high-entropy alloys.
Suitable initial specimens include cast or additively manufactured high-entropy alloys.
The initial solid HEA specimens are metastable.
Equiatomic or near-equiatomic CoCrCuNi is an example composition to which the approach applies.
HEA samples can be heated in a high-temperature furnace while neutron imaging is performed in situ.
Calorimetric measurements can be performed simultaneously with in-situ neutron imaging under the proposed setup.
Experimental observations can be calibrated and validated using third-generation CALPHAD predictions.
Real-time heating and cooling measurements over approximately 1000 °C to 1500 °C can cover melting and solidification behavior in CoCrCu-based HEAs.
A controlled atmosphere avoids oxidation during the high-temperature measurements.
Neutron imaging can observe melting, liquid-phase separation or remixing, and solidification in real time.
Neutron imaging can quantitatively capture the volume change associated with melting.
Observed liquid-phase behavior correlates directly with atomic-level structural changes that control fusion thermodynamics.
Simultaneous calorimetry records the energy absorbed or released during melting and solidification.
Combining imaging and calorimetry with refined CALPHAD reduces uncertainty in fusion enthalpy, entropy, and volume-change estimates.
Third-generation CALPHAD descriptions can reliably represent solid- and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties over broad composition and temperature ranges.
Predicted melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and melting volume change will agree with experimental values within about 5–10%.
The integrated method is more efficient than separate calorimetry and post-mortem structural analysis.
Traditional separate measurements have greater uncertainty because of phase separation and metastability.
The method is most effective for single-phase or compositionally homogeneous HEA melts and may be limited by extensive liquid immiscibility or rapid phase kinetics.
Consistent deviations greater than approximately 10% for a significant subset of compositions, or failure to image the expected fusion-related phase behavior, would falsify the integrated approach.
